To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Treg expansion is driven by HIV infection, not by aging, in HIV-infected adults.

(i) HIV-infected adults and children have similar Treg frequency; (ii) Treg frequency is similar in HIV-infected children and adults, but it is higher in both groups than that found in HIV-uninfected adults.

1) HIV infection, not aging, directly drives the Treg expansion seen in older HIVinfected subjects; 2) this effect is not mediated by the viral load, as it occurs in HIV-infected children with similar viral load levels than HIV-infected adults; 3) this Treg expansion may contribute to the immune dysfunction observed in older HIV-infested subjects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of age and duration of HIV-infection on Treg compartment.
the question of whether age or HIV is the driving factor in Treg compartment changes that occur in HIV-infected persons.
a cross-sectional study that includes HIV-infected adults and children with similar duration of viral exposure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Treg expansion seen in aged HIV-inflicted subjects is likely driven by HIV infection, not by aging, and that the CD4+ Treg phenotype should be used in future studies.
age-related changes in regulatory T-cells are not the same as those seen in healthy individuals and HIV infection is likely the driving force behind the changes observed in HIV-infected persons.
HIV-infected persons have a higher Treg compartment that may be due to HIV effects, but the effect of age cannot be excluded
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV progression is the main driver of Treg expansion in HIV-infected persons.
Treg compartment is not affected by age in HIV infection but by HIV progression, and that the expansion of Treg cells in HIV-infected persons is a direct consequence of HIV viral exposure.
Treg frequency in HIV-infected children is similar to that found in healthy children and adults, and Treg frequencies in HIV-infected adults are similar to that found among healthy adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Treg compartment is not affected by aging in HIV-infector subjects.
Treg frequency was not higher in the older group of HIVinfected subjects, despite their lower CD4 T-cell count, but was significantly lower in vertically HIV-infected children.
the expansion of Tregs in aged HIV-inflicted subjects is likely due to HIV infection, not to age, and that the Treg expansion is associated to a lower immune activation.
